observations.notes: About 1 in 4 people on Earth is under 15. High birth rates in Africa and South Asia keep this number significant, though it has fallen from 1 in 3 just 50 years ago.

entity.name: Children under 15
entity.description: People aged 0-14

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: Children under 15 make up about 1 in 4 people globally, but the proportion varies hugely — from over 40% in some African countries to under 15% in aging European nations

observations.notes: Around 10% of the world is over 65 — a proportion that will double by 2050 as populations in wealthy nations age rapidly.

entity.name: People over 65
entity.description: People aged 65 and over

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: The share of people over 65 is rising in almost every country — driven by falling birth rates and longer lives — creating new pressures on pension and healthcare systems

observations.notes: For the first time in history, more than half of humanity lives in urban areas. By 2050 that will be closer to 700 out of 1,000.

entity.name: Urban residents
entity.description: People living in cities or urban areas

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: Lagos, Dhaka, and Delhi each add millions of residents every year — cities in the global south now account for most of the world's urban population
In 1950 only about 30 in every 100 people lived in cities; by 2050 that figure is expected to reach 68 — urbanisation is one of the defining shifts of the modern era
More than half of humanity now lives in cities, a proportion that was under 30% in 1950 — and urbanisation continues fastest in Africa and Asia

observations.notes: The world has about 4 doctors per 1,000 people globally, but this hides enormous inequality — some wealthy nations have 35 per 1,000 while some low-income nations have fewer than 0.2.

entity.name: Doctors
entity.description: Registered medical doctors worldwide

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: The US alone has more registered doctors than all of sub-Saharan Africa combined
Most of the world's doctors are clustered in wealthy countries — sub-Saharan Africa has less than 3% of global physicians despite 16% of the world's population
Norway has 40 doctors per 1,000 people; Niger has fewer than 0.1
Global physician numbers have grown 60% since 2000, but mostly in countries that were already well-supplied
The world has about 4 doctors per 1,000 people on average, but this average hides enormous inequality between wealthy and low-income nations

observations.notes: There are roughly 10 nurses and midwives per 1,000 people globally, forming the backbone of healthcare in most of the world.

entity.name: Nurses and midwives
entity.description: Registered nurses and midwives worldwide

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: Sub-Saharan Africa faces a shortage of over 4 million nurses — its healthcare systems rely heavily on community health workers who have no formal nursing qualification
Nurses and midwives outnumber doctors roughly two to one globally, and in many rural areas they are the only healthcare providers that communities ever see

observations.notes: Roughly 70 million primary school teachers serve the world's 700 million primary-age students — an average class size of about 24, though in many regions classes have 50+ students.

entity.name: Primary school teachers
entity.description: Teachers working at primary school level

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: Sub-Saharan Africa will need to hire around 17 million more teachers by 2030 just to achieve universal primary education — a goal many countries are far from reaching
About 70 million primary school teachers serve the world's youngest learners, but shortages are acute in sub-Saharan Africa where some schools have one teacher for 60 or more children

observations.notes: About 28% of the global workforce is in agriculture, mostly smallholder farmers in Asia and Africa. In wealthy nations this figure is under 5%.

entity.name: Agricultural workers
entity.description: People working in agriculture farming fishing or forestry

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: More than 90% of the world's farms are smallholdings under 2 hectares — most are in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, where agriculture remains the primary livelihood for billions
Despite making up over a quarter of the global workforce, farmers — mostly smallholders in Asia and Africa — are disproportionately represented among the world's poorest people

observations.notes: Around 700–900 million people live on less than $2.15 per day (2017 PPP). This figure has fallen dramatically — it was over 1,900 per 1,000 in 1990.

entity.name: People in extreme poverty
entity.description: People living on under $2.15 per day

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: More than 90% of people in extreme poverty live in sub-Saharan Africa or South Asia — in some countries more than half the population lives below the $2.15-a-day line
The share of people in extreme poverty fell from nearly 40% in 1990 to under 10% by 2019 — then stalled as COVID-19, conflict, and climate disruption reversed progress in many regions
About 9 in 10 extremely poor people live in sub-Saharan Africa or South Asia — a geographic concentration that shapes where foreign aid and development programs focus

observations.notes: About two-thirds of humanity is now online. The remaining third — mostly in rural sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia — are the focus of major connectivity efforts.

entity.name: Internet users
entity.description: People with access to the internet

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: India crossed 800 million internet users in 2023 — a single country now has more people online than the entire world did in 2005
Internet access grew from fewer than 2% of the global population in 1997 to about 67% today — one of the fastest diffusions of any technology in history
Internet access has grown faster than almost any technology in history — from fewer than 1 in 50 people in 1997 to roughly 2 in 3 today — yet the last third remain largely offline

observations.notes: More than half of all people now carry a smartphone — a technology that barely existed 20 years ago. Mobile phones have leapfrogged wired infrastructure in the developing world.

entity.name: Smartphone owners
entity.description: People who own a smartphone

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: China and India together account for roughly a third of all smartphone users on Earth — scale in just two countries that dwarfs most continents
More people now own a smartphone than have access to safely managed drinking water — a striking illustration of how consumer technology has outpaced basic infrastructure

observations.notes: Global adult literacy stands at around 87%. The 13% who cannot read are concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and among women in conservative regions.

entity.name: Literate adults
entity.description: Adults who can read and write

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: About two-thirds of the world's 770 million illiterate adults are women — and most are concentrated in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa
Global adult literacy has risen from roughly 56% in 1970 to 87% today, one of the most consistent improvements in human capability over the past half-century

observations.notes: The world produces enough food — about 2,850 calories per person per day — to feed everyone. Hunger persists due to distribution failures, poverty, and waste, not global scarcity.

entity.name: Daily food calories available
entity.description: Calories available per person per day from food supply

metric.name: Per-capita daily rate
metric.description: Quantity consumed or available per person per day

facts: The United States throws away enough food each year to provide every American with 1,400 calories a day — while 700 million people globally go to bed hungry

The world produces enough calories to feed every person — the challenge is that food is unevenly distributed, with wealthy populations consuming far more than they need while hundreds of millions go hungry

observations.notes: About 1.3 billion tonnes of food — roughly one-third of all food produced — is wasted each year. In wealthy nations most waste is at the consumer end; in poor nations it's mostly post-harvest losses.

entity.name: Annual food wasted
entity.description: Food lost or wasted globally per year

metric.name: Annual total flow
metric.description: Total quantity produced or lost per year globally

facts: The food wasted globally each year would be enough to feed every hungry person on Earth more than twice over
In high-income countries, most food is wasted at the retail and consumer stage; in low-income countries, losses happen mostly at harvest, storage, and transport
North Americans and Europeans waste roughly 95–115 kg of food per person per year, compared to just 6–11 kg per person in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia
Food waste has barely declined in wealthy nations despite decades of awareness campaigns — reducing it remains one of the cheapest ways to cut agricultural emissions

observations.notes: The global average is about 185 liters per person per day across all uses (drinking, cooking, sanitation, agriculture). Americans use ~500 liters; many Africans survive on under 20 liters.

entity.name: Daily freshwater consumption
entity.description: Freshwater used per person per day across all uses

metric.name: Per-capita daily rate
metric.description: Quantity consumed or available per person per day

facts: Agriculture accounts for about 70% of all freshwater withdrawals globally — meaning the water footprint of food production dwarfs household consumption
Americans use roughly 500 litres of water per day; people in Mozambique or Niger typically use under 20 litres — enough for drinking but little else
About 70% of all freshwater humans use goes to agriculture — meaning the water footprint of food is far larger than what comes out of household taps

observations.notes: About 2.2 billion people lack access to safely managed drinking water. This is one of the most preventable causes of death and disease worldwide.

entity.name: People without safe drinking water
entity.description: People lacking safely managed drinking water

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for about a third of the global population without safe water, followed by South Asia — together these two regions hold most of the world's water-insecure people
Most people without safe water live in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia — and the burden falls disproportionately on women and girls who walk hours daily to collect it

observations.notes: The average person uses about 3,300 kWh of electricity per year. Americans use ~12,000 kWh; the global average hides vast inequality — an American uses 10× more than someone in Ethiopia.

entity.name: Annual electricity consumed

metric.description: Quantity consumed or available per person per year

facts: If the world's electricity were divided equally, each person's share would be enough for basic lighting and a phone charger — but far less than a typical American household uses
Sub-Saharan Africa generates about 1% of global electricity despite holding roughly 15% of the world's population
An average American uses about 10 times more electricity per year than an average person in Ethiopia
Global electricity demand has more than doubled since 1990, driven by population growth, industrialisation in Asia, and the rise of consumer electronics

observations.notes: About 30% of global electricity now comes from renewable sources (hydro, wind, solar, etc.). This share is rising rapidly — wind and solar alone exceeded 13% in 2023.

entity.name: Renewable electricity share
entity.description: Share of electricity generated from renewable sources

metric.name: Percentage share
metric.description: Fraction of a whole expressed per 1000 units

facts: China installed more solar capacity in 2023 than the entire world had installed in all years up to 2022 — the energy transition is accelerating faster than most forecasts predicted
The share of renewables in global electricity has roughly doubled since 2010, driven mostly by the dramatic fall in wind and solar costs — both now cheaper than new coal in most markets
Solar energy is growing faster than any fuel in history — capacity added globally in 2023 exceeded all previous records, mostly driven by China, the US, and Europe

observations.notes: About 730 million people — mostly in sub-Saharan Africa and developing Asia — still have no access to electricity. This number has fallen from 1.2 billion in 2010.

entity.description: People lacking any access to electricity

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: About 80% of people without electricity live in sub-Saharan Africa — a region with some of the best solar resources on Earth yet the least access to modern energy
The 730 million people without electricity are concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia — and for many, cooking with solid fuels causes more immediate harm than lack of light

observations.notes: An estimated 1.6 billion people live in inadequate housing — slums, informal settlements, or without any shelter. This includes 100 million who are literally homeless.

entity.description: People living in slums informal settlements or without shelter

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: Mumbai's Dharavi neighbourhood — one of the world's largest slums — packs over a million people into less than 2 square kilometres, illustrating how acute urban housing pressure can become
An estimated 1.6 billion people live in inadequate housing, including slums and informal settlements — yet only about 100 million are literally without any shelter

observations.notes: There are roughly 1.45 billion cars on Earth — about 1 for every 5 people. But car ownership is extremely unequal: the US has ~800 cars per 1,000 people; India has about 30.

facts: The US has about 800 cars for every 1,000 people; India has about 30 — a ratio that reflects not just wealth but also the quality of public transport infrastructure
The wealthiest 10% of countries account for roughly 70% of all cars on the road — car ownership remains heavily concentrated in North America, Europe, and parts of East Asia
There are more cars on Earth than there are people in China and India combined, yet the vast majority are owned by people in just a handful of wealthy nations

observations.notes: About 1.5 billion people took at least one commercial flight in 2023 (IATA). That's 150 out of every 1,000 people on Earth who fly at least once per year — flying remains a minority activity, heavily concentrated in wealthy countries.

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts: The US alone accounts for roughly a quarter of all commercial passengers globally — more than all of Africa, South America, and the Middle East combined
About 80% of the world's population has never been on a plane — flying is overwhelmingly the activity of a relatively small, relatively wealthy global minority
Flying remains one of the most unequally distributed activities on Earth — the majority of flights are taken by a small minority of frequent flyers, mostly in wealthy countries

observations.notes: The global average GDP per capita is about $13,500/year, but the median person earns far less. The US average is ~$65,000; the average in low-income countries is under $1,000.

entity.name: GDP per capita

metric.description: Quantity consumed or available per person per year

facts: Luxembourg's GDP per capita exceeds $120,000 per year; Burundi's is under $300 — a 400-fold gap that illustrates how little the global average tells you about any individual country
The average person in the world's 10 richest countries earns roughly 50 times more than the average person in the 10 poorest — a gap that has barely narrowed in decades
The global average GDP per capita is pulled up by high-income countries — the median person on Earth earns far less, closer to $5,000–6,000 per year

observations.notes: The wealthiest 10% of people hold about 76% of all global wealth. The bottom 50% hold less than 2%. Wealth inequality is far more extreme than income inequality.

entity.description: Share of all global wealth held by the wealthiest 10%

metric.name: Percentage share

facts: The wealth of the world's ten richest individuals exceeds the combined wealth of the poorest 40% of humanity
North America and Europe together hold more than 60% of all global household wealth, despite containing less than 20% of the world's population
The bottom 50% of humanity — about 4 billion people — collectively hold less than 2% of all global wealth
Wealth inequality worsened after the 2008 financial crisis as stock and property prices recovered faster than wages, benefiting those who already owned assets

observations.notes: The world loses about 47 million hectares of forest each year — an area the size of Sweden — though reforestation efforts offset some of this.

metric.name: Annual total flow
metric.description: Total quantity produced or lost per year globally

facts: Brazil, Indonesia, and the Democratic Republic of Congo together account for more than half of all tropical deforestation — three countries defining the pace of global forest loss

Brazil's Amazon deforestation fell by roughly 80% between 2004 and 2012 under strong enforcement policies — then rebounded sharply when those policies weakened, showing deforestation is a political choice
Tropical forests are disappearing fastest — Brazil, Indonesia, and the Democratic Republic of Congo account for a large share of global deforestation, mostly driven by agriculture

observations.notes: The average person emits about 4.6 tonnes of CO₂ per year. Americans emit ~14 tonnes; people in the poorest countries emit under 0.5 tonnes — a 30× gap.

facts: A return economy-class flight from London to New York emits roughly 1 tonne of CO₂ per passenger — about as much as an average person in Rwanda emits in an entire year
The richest 10% of people are responsible for about half of all global carbon emissions, while the poorest 50% produce less than 10% — climate change is driven mostly by the wealthy
The richest 10% of people are responsible for about half of all global carbon emissions, while the poorest 50% produce less than 10%

observations.notes: The global average life expectancy is 73 years — up from 48 in 1950. Japan leads at 84; some low-income nations are still under 60.

entity.name: Life expectancy at birth
entity.description: Average number of years a newborn is expected to live

metric.name: Per-capita annual rate

facts: Japan leads global life expectancy at around 84 years; Chad sits at around 54 years — a 30-year gap that reflects differences in healthcare, nutrition, water, and conflict
Global life expectancy rose from 48 years in 1950 to 73 today — one of the most dramatic improvements in human welfare ever measured, driven mainly by reductions in child mortality
Life expectancy at birth has risen by 25 years globally since 1950, mostly due to better child survival — but the gap between the richest and poorest countries remains over 20 years

observations.notes: About 260 million children and youth are out of school. Most are in conflict-affected zones or the most remote rural areas of sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.

facts: More than half of out-of-school children live in conflict-affected countries — places where schools have been destroyed, teachers have fled, and families are displaced
About 260 million children are out of school globally, most concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia — regions where poverty, conflict, and gender inequality compound one another

observations.notes: Over 114 million people are forcibly displaced — including 36 million refugees who have fled their home countries — the highest figure ever recorded.

The number of forcibly displaced people has more than doubled since 2012, driven by prolonged conflicts that show no sign of resolution — displacement is increasingly long-term, not temporary
Over 114 million people are forcibly displaced globally — including 36 million refugees who have fled their home countries — the highest figure ever recorded
